title: User-Requested Performance Counters
why: Documents optional PMU-backed hardware performance counters and their libpfm/platform requirements, which chapter 1 needs alongside benchmark-supplied user counters to distinguish counted logical bytes from independently measured hardware events.

claim: In a program with spatial locality, most addresses accessed are spatially local to the address accessed just before.
quote: programs where most addresses accessed are spatially local to the address accessed before them.

claim: Caches typically fetch nearby addresses along with an accessed address, on the assumption that those nearby addresses will soon be accessed.
quote: When caching memory, it is typical to remember not just the exact memory accesses but also the memory nearby, on the assumption (based on spatial locality) that if one address is accessed, nearby addresses will soon be accessed as well.

claim: A benchmark can discard an initial warmup period, which may be necessary for code that needs to fill some form of cache before its performance is of interest.
quote: Minimum number of seconds a benchmark should be run before results should be taken into account. This can be necessary for benchmarks of code which needs to fill some form of cache before performance is of interest. Results gathered within this period are discarded and not used for the reported result.

locator: Statistics: Reporting the Mean, Median and Standard Deviation / Coefficient of variation of Repeated Benchmarks
claim: Because a single benchmark result may be unrepresentative when timings are noisy, a benchmark can be run repeatedly.
quote: However benchmarks are often noisy and a single result may not be representative of the overall behavior. For this reason it’s possible to repeatedly rerun the benchmark.

claim: The median is the value that has half the data smaller and half the data larger.
quote: median - the median is the value of the point which has half the data smaller than that point and half the data larger than that point.

claim: MAD is the median of the absolute deviations of the observations from the data's median, and it is less affected by extremes in the tail than the average absolute deviation because tail values influence a median less than a mean.
quote:
- \( MAD = median (|Y_{i} - \tilde{Y}|) \)

where \(\tilde{Y}\) is the median of the data and |Y| is the absolute value of Y. This is a variation of the average absolute deviation that is even less affected by extremes in the tail because the data in the tails have less influence on the calculation of the median than they do on the mean.

claim: DoNotOptimize does not prevent the compiler from optimizing its expression, and the expression may be removed entirely when its result is already known.
quote: Note that DoNotOptimize(<expr>) does not prevent optimizations on <expr> in any way. <expr> may even be removed entirely when the result is already known.

claim: By default the whole work loop is timed; work inside the loop can be excluded from the measurement with pause/resume, but that is not recommended because it has high overhead.
quote: Normally, the entire duration of the work loop (for (auto _ : state) {}) is measured. But sometimes, it is necessary to do some work inside of that loop, every iteration, but without counting that time to the benchmark time. That is possible, although it is not recommended, since it has high overhead.

claim: CLOCK_MONOTONIC readings never go backwards, but on some architectures consecutive reads can return the same value.
quote: All CLOCK_MONOTONIC variants guarantee that the time returned by consecutive calls will not go backwards, but successive calls may—depending on the architecture—return identical (not-increased) time values.

claim: perf_counter returns fractional seconds from a clock with the highest available resolution for short durations, includes time spent sleeping, and has an undefined reference point, so only differences between readings are meaningful.
quote: Return the value (in fractional seconds) of a performance counter, i.e. a clock with the highest available resolution to measure a short duration. It does include time elapsed during sleep. The clock is the same for all processes. The reference point of the returned value is undefined, so that only the difference between the results of two calls is valid.

locator: Reducing Variance in Benchmarks, list of sources of variance, item 1
claim: Repeated runs on a multi-core machine can differ because not all CPUs, cores, or hardware threads run at the same speed.
quote: On multi-core machines not all CPUs/CPU cores/CPU threads run the same speed, so running a benchmark one time and then again may give a different result depending on which CPU it ran on.

claim: Changing the experimental setup often leads to contradictory conclusions about how much the O3 optimization level speeds a program up.
quote:
We show that changing the experimental setup often leads
to contradictory conclusions about the speedup of O3.

locator: Output Formats, JSON format, context object
claim: A benchmark report's context object records run metadata such as date, host, CPU, caches, load average, and library version, and extra custom context can be added to it.
quote: The context object contains information about the run in general, including the date, host, CPU, caches, load average, benchmark library version, and json_schema_version. Extra context added with benchmark::AddCustomContext or --benchmark_context is emitted as additional string fields in context.

claim: The benchmark program supplies the byte count to SetBytesProcessed itself, here iterations times the bytes per iteration.
Collecting hardware performance counters requires a machine with a Performance Monitoring Unit and a build with counter support, currently via libpfm.
quote:
This feature is available if:

- The benchmark is run on an architecture featuring a Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU),

- The benchmark is compiled with support for collecting counters. Currently, this requires libpfm, which is built as a dependency via Bazel.
